title: Where the Sun stops setting
hook: In June the far north gets a Sun that never sets. Where exactly does that start?

knows: that days are long in northern summer
that the Earth's axis is tilted
doesNotKnow: the latitude where the Sun stops setting on the solstice
that it is 90 degrees minus the tilt

misconception: The Sun stays up all day only at the poles, or only well past the Arctic Circle.
objective: The learner can explain that on the June solstice the Sun does not set north of 90 - 23.4 = 66.6 N, because the night side's edge stops that far short of the pole.

claims.text: On the June solstice the Sun does not set north of about 66.6 N, which is 90 degrees minus the tilt of about 23.4 degrees; the reveal places it between the highest latitude where the learner saw a sunset and the lowest where they saw none (computed by dayHours() in Demo.tsx).
claims.source: Day length from cos(H) = -tan(lat) tan(dec) with dec = 23.44 (obliquity, IAU / Astronomical Almanac, from memory): H reaches 180 degrees (24 h of day) when lat >= 90 - 23.44 = 66.56. Geometric centre of the Sun, airless spherical Earth. Computed in Demo.tsx. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node of dayHours(): 24 h first at 66.56 N (66.5 gives 23.42 h; first 0.1 slider step with 24 h is 66.6); 90-23.44 = 66.56 shown as 66.6. Since sets < 66.56 <= never, the reveal's line always lies between the two quoted latitudes. Obliquity 23.44 (IAU 2006: 23.4393 at J2000) correct to my knowledge.

claims.text: In this model, at 65.0 N the solstice day is 21 h 07 min long.
claims.source: Same formula, lat = 65: cos(H) = -tan 65 x tan 23.44 = -0.931, H = 158.6 degrees, day = 2H/15 = 21.1 h. Computed live in Demo.tsx (scratch b.mjs agrees: 21.12 h).

claims.text: The line at 66.6 N is the Arctic Circle.
claims.source: The Arctic Circle is defined as the parallel at 90 degrees minus the obliquity, about 66.56 N today (Astronomical Almanac; any atlas). From memory, not checked online. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. Claim wording unchanged; the reveal sentence now reads 'That line is the Arctic Circle, not the Tropic of Cancer (23.4°N), ...'. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): LEFT UNVERIFIED, not disputed. Stage check passes: the reveal's 'That line is the Arctic Circle' follows P1's 'The line between is about 66.6°N' (LINE = 90 - 23.44 = 66.56, shown 66.6; node). The claim is a naming convention and rests on a reference (Astronomical Almanac / atlas) that I could not open this session (web fetch fails DNS; search snippets are not an opened source). Previous verification was from memory. Needs a fact-checker re-check with an opened reference.

claims.text: Because air bends sunlight and the Sun is a disc, the real midnight Sun can be seen a little south of the line.
claims.source: Standard sunrise/sunset is defined at a Sun-centre altitude of -0.833 degrees (34 arcmin refraction plus 16 arcmin semi-diameter; USNO / Astronomical Almanac). With that, the solstice midnight Sun reaches roughly 65.7 N. From memory, not checked online; the lesson gives no number for it. | WITHDRAWN 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): cm-geography cut the no-air caveat from the reveal; no learner-visible sentence carries this claim now (the stage caption keeps only 'Toy: no air', a model label). Fact-checker to confirm the withdrawal. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): WITHDRAWAL CONFIRMED. Demo.tsx v4 read on every path: no learner-visible sentence says air bends sunlight or that the midnight Sun is seen south of the line. The caption 'Toy: no air' is a model label, not this claim.

claims.text: 23.4 N is the Tropic of Cancer, where the Sun is directly overhead at noon on the June solstice; the Arctic Circle is a different line. Around June 21 is the longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere (predict question).
claims.source: Standard geography references (Tropic of Cancer at the Sun-declination limit of about 23.44 N; June solstice about 21 June). · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Tropic latitude = solar declination limit (23.44 N); on the June solstice the subsolar point is at the declination, so noon Sun is overhead there. "June 21": the solstice falls on June 20-22 depending on year and time zone; declination one day off the solstice differs by 0.0035 deg, so day length differs by seconds. Suggest "around June 21" if the builder touches the text. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. Reveal now carries the Tropic as a clause; 'around June 21' per pass 19. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): DISPUTED. The stage makes two claims different from the text. (1) The predict question reads 'June 21 is the longest day in the north.' with no hedge; the claim says 'Around June 21'. Opened source: astronomy-engine 2.1.19 Seasons() (npm tarball, read and run locally) puts the June solstice at 2024-06-20 20:51 UTC and 2028-06-20 20:02 UTC (June 20 in UTC; in the Americas in more years), so the flat date is false in some years. Fix: 'Around June 21 the north has its longest day.' (2) The reveal clause 'the Tropic of Cancer (23.4°N), where the noon Sun is overhead' drops 'on the June solstice': read alone it says the noon Sun is always overhead there. astronomy-engine: noon zenith distance at 23.44 N is 0.00 on 2026-06-21, 1.35 deg on 06-01, 23.2 deg at the September equinox. Fix: '..., where the noon Sun is overhead that day.' (+2 words, about 83, under 90). The numbers hold: solstice Sun declination 23.436-23.439 (2000-2028), shown 23.4. Also, the Tropic of Cancer name is a convention whose reference I could not open; after the fix this needs a re-check with an opened reference.

claims.text: The day strip shows, hour by hour on the solstice, when the Sun is above the horizon at the town (yellow), computed from the angular distance between the town and the Sun point at 23.44 N.
claims.source: strip in Demo.tsx uses geoDistance(town, subsolar point) < 90 degrees for each hour; same model as the Daylight readout.

claims.text: In June the north pole leans 23.4 degrees toward the Sun, so the night side's edge stops 23.4 degrees short of the pole (the orange gap on the globe); a town whose daily circle fits inside the gap stays lit all day.
claims.source: The night side is the 90-degree circle centred on the antisolar point at 23.44 S; along its meridian it reaches 90 − 23.44 = 66.56 N, leaving 23.44 degrees to the pole. Geometry in Demo.tsx (night, gap). Reveal paragraph 2. | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: a 90-degree circle centred at 23.44 S reaches at most 66.56 N, on the antisolar meridian, leaving 23.44 degrees to the pole; any parallel above it is wholly lit. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. Text shortened to match reveal paragraph 2. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): VERIFIED. Independent of the drafter (text cm-geography W-266, applied by demo-builder). Stage: reveal P2 'the pole leans 23.4° toward the Sun, so the night side's edge stops 23.4° short of it. A town whose circle fits inside the gap stays lit all day.' matches the claim; the orange gap ('23.4° gap = tilt', pole dot) is drawn after the lock, so it is on the stage when the reveal points at it. Node (d3-geo): the night circle centred at 23.44 S reaches 66.56 N on the antisolar meridian (distance 90.000 deg), leaving 23.44 deg to the pole; parallels at 66.57, 66.6, 70, 80 N are lit at every longitude, 66.5 is not. Opened source for the 23.4: astronomy-engine 2.1.19 mean_obliq() uses 84381.406 arcsec (IAU 2006) = 23.4393 deg at J2000; computed solstice Sun declination 23.436-23.439 for 2000-2028. Nit, not blocking: the claim says 'In June'; the lean is 23.4 only near the solstice (22.09 deg on June 1, astronomy-engine); 'On the June solstice' would be exact. The learner-visible sentence has no date and sits on a solstice globe.

recall.question: If the Earth's axis were tilted 30 degrees instead of 23.4, where would the June midnight Sun begin?
recall.why: The night side's edge stops one tilt short of the pole, so the Sun stops setting at 90 minus the tilt: 90 - 30 = 60 N.
